head.h1: Jain Catering in Dubai — What It Costs and How to Book

opening_paragraph: Jain catering in Dubai serves fully Jain-compliant vegetarian food — strictly no onion, garlic or root vegetables — from AED 700 per person, quoted to your guest count, menu and service style. A Jain table isn't ordinary vegetarian food with a few swaps: it excludes underground vegetables (potato, onion, garlic, ginger, carrot, beetroot), honey and often after-dark cooking, and it needs a kitchen that keeps those rules without a single lapse. MyCHEF pairs you with a vetted chef who plans the jain menu dubai families recognise, cooks on site and clears away afterward. Send your date, numbers and venue and, during our published business hours, you'll have a proposal you can read back promptly.

new_paragraphs: A Jain menu is built entirely without onion, garlic, ginger or root vegetables, using above-ground produce, pulses, grains and dairy to carry the flavour instead. Typical dishes we design around include Jain thalis and sabzis, dal without garlic tempering, paneer and vegetable curries seasoned with asafoetida and spice blends instead of onion-garlic bases, farsan and satvik snacks, and mithai and sweets made without honey. Rotis, puris, khichdi, dhokla and fresh salads round out a full spread. Everything is prepared satvik, with separate oil and utensils. Jain catering packages dubai clients choose from range from a simple plated three-course dinner to an elaborate festival buffet, and every jain menu dubai option is bespoke — nothing is off a fixed list. If a family follows an even stricter interpretation (no leafy greens during Paryushan, for instance), we confirm and honour it before the event.

add_block.new_heading: The full Jain catering menu, course by course
new_paragraphs: This is the working dish bank the chefs build from, set out in the order a Jain table runs — welcome drink, farsan, chaat, starters, dal, paneer, a seasonal vegetable, rice, bread, raita and mithai. A buffet usually takes four to eight items per course; a thali or plated dinner takes one or two and goes deeper on each. Nothing here is a fixed package. You mark what your family wants, the chef says what is at its peak that week, and the agreed list goes into the written quote before anything is confirmed.

One structural point shapes everything below: a Jain menu is re-engineered, not stripped. The good versions name what replaced what. Jain Pav Bhaji is built on raw banana in place of potato. Gatte ki Sabji, besan dumplings in a yoghurt gravy, sits where a root-vegetable sabzi would. Asafoetida and roasted spice blends carry the base note that onion and garlic carry in an ordinary Indian kitchen. Any dish whose standard version leans on potato, onion, garlic, ginger, carrot or beetroot is either rebuilt that way or left off your list, and the chef tells you which, dish by dish, before you approve the menu.

What is controlled and what is not, stated plainly: your Jain requirements go to the assigned culinary partner in writing before the event — no onion, garlic, ginger or root vegetables, no honey, eggless throughout — with separate utensils, fresh oil, dedicated prep surfaces and an agreed cooking sequence for your booking. Partner kitchens also handle allergens and non-Jain ingredients for other work, so cross-contact cannot be completely excluded unless dedicated controls have been specifically confirmed for your event. Guests with allergies must give full details before confirming. Volume formats start at 10 guests, buffets at 20, with a minimum order of AED 900.

If you are searching for a Jain restaurant in Dubai instead, the pure-veg and sattvic kitchens cluster around Bur Dubai and Karama, and several run no-onion-no-garlic as the house default. A restaurant seats your family; catering brings the same discipline to your hall, villa, temple gathering or office at your own guest count, on your own timing. Both have their place — this page is about the second.
Welcome drinks and chaas
One drink is normally included and poured as guests arrive; larger events take two.
Kesariya Lassi: saffron and cardamom lassi, thick enough to eat with a spoon.
Mango Lassi: yoghurt and ripe mango, the reliable crowd-pleaser.
Govindas Thandai: chilled milk with almonds, fennel and cracked pepper.
Buttermilk (chaas): salted and cumin-scented, the traditional Jain table drink.
Classic Lemonade: fresh lemon and mint, built without ginger.
Fresh juices and smoothies: seasonal fruit, pressed the same day.
Rabri Faluda: rose syrup, vermicelli and reduced milk — half drink, half dessert.
Farsan: the Gujarati and Rajasthani snack bank
Farsan is where a Jain menu is strongest, because most of it is Jain by construction — gram flour, pulses and above-ground vegetables, no root, no onion base.
Khaman Dhokla: soft yellow gram-flour squares, tempered with mustard and curry leaf.
Edada Dhokla: steamed and coarser, served warm with green chutney.
Sandwich Dhokla: layered white and yellow, cut into batons for a tray.
Khandvi: rolled gram-flour ribbons with coconut and coriander.
Handvo: savoury baked lentil and bottle-gourd cake with a crisp seed crust.
Patra: colocasia leaves rolled with spiced besan, sliced and tempered.
Sev Khamni: crumbled khaman under a shower of fine sev.
Cut Mirchi: split green chillies in a light batter, for guests who want heat.
Dal Vada: crunchy split-lentil fritters, ground coarse.
Bajri Vada: pearl-millet fritters, a Kathiawadi winter favourite.
Masala Vada: spiced chana dal patties, fried to order.
Kothimbir Vadi: coriander and besan steamed, then shallow-fried.
Fafda / Papdi Gathiya: the Sunday-morning Gujarati pairing, with papaya chutney.
Lilva Kachori: green pigeon-pea filling, sweet and hot at once.
Khasta Kachori: flaky shell over a dry lentil filling.
Marwari Kachori: Rajasthani-style, heavier spiced, meant to be broken and topped.
Green Pea Kachori: pea and coconut filling, lighter than the lentil version.
Idli with Chutney: steamed, for a breakfast or early-lunch spread.
The Jain chaat counter
Chaat is worth running as its own counter instead of folding it into starters. Every item below is built without potato or onion — moong, raw banana and boiled chana carry the fillings instead.
Pani Puri / Golgappa: filled with moong and spiced water, no potato.
Sev Puri: flat puris, chutneys and sev, assembled to order.
Bhel Puri: puffed rice and papdi, tossed dry so it stays crisp.
Dahi Puri: yoghurt, sweet tamarind and green chutney in one bite.
Papdi Chaat: crisp papdi under yoghurt and chutneys.
Raj Kachori: the large stuffed kachori, built Jain and eaten with a spoon.
Dahi Bhalla: lentil dumplings soaked and dressed in sweetened yoghurt.
Samosa Chaat: Jain samosa broken under chole and chutney.
Dahi Chana Chat: chana, yoghurt and pomegranate, the mildest option on the counter.
Jain Pav Bhaji: raw banana in place of potato, no onion in the mash or the garnish.
Hot starters and tandoor
Four to six of these fill a starter round. The fried items want cooking on site, not delivering.
Vegetable Samosa: Jain filling of peas, paneer and spice, no potato.
Punjabi Samosa: the larger, thicker-shelled version.
Hara Bara Kebab: spinach, peas and chana, bound with besan instead of potato.
Vegetable Pakora: batter-fried seasonal above-ground vegetables.
Vegetable Shami Kabab: soft chana-dal patties, griddled.
Vegetable Kathi Roll: paratha wrapped around a spiced filling, cut into thirds.
Paneer Poppers: cubes in a crisp coating, one of the few things every child eats.
Paneer Malai Tikka: cream and cardamom marinade, off the tandoor.
Chilli Cheese Toast: grilled, cut small, gone first.
Dry Gobi Manchurian: cauliflower tossed in a Jain Indo-Chinese sauce.
Vegetable Spring Roll: shredded cabbage and beans, no onion in the filling.
Vegetable Puffs: flaky pastry, served warm from the box.
Crispy Baked Zucchini Fries: baked, not fried, for a lighter tray.
Vegetable Tempura: light batter, an Asian counterpoint to the Indian tray.
Grilled Halloumi with Cherry Tomato: skewered, off the grill.
Assorted Mini Pizzas (Vegetable / Margharita): for mixed-age gatherings.
Hot Spinach Rolls with Cheese: filled and baked, cut on the bias.
Breaded Risotto Balls: crisp outside, molten inside.
Cold canapés for a standing reception

For a launch, an engagement or a reception where nobody sits down. Six to eight varieties is the usual order. Where a classic recipe uses garlic — hummus, pesto — it is rebuilt without it for a Jain brief.
Canapé Chaat in Taco Cups: chaat, contained, eaten in one.
Paneer Potli with Mint Chutney in Shots: little parcels with chutney beneath.
Mini Hummus & Roasted Pepper Phyllo Bites: garlic-free hummus in crisp phyllo.
Spinach Artichoke Stuffed Mushrooms: warm-served but works cold.
Vine Leaves Tzatziki in Shooters: rolled leaf standing in cucumber yoghurt.
Stuffed Vine Leaves: rice and herb filling, lemon-dressed.
Buffalo Mozzarella with Cherry Tomato & Pesto Sauce in Shots.
Roast Tomato Caprese with Basil Leaves & Cheese.
Tomato, Mozzarella & Basil Bruschetta: assembled late so it stays crisp.
Grilled Zucchini with Light Philadelphia Cheese: rolled and skewered.
Cucumber Mint Gazpacho with Sour Cream in Shots: the summer opener.
Crisp vegetable tarts: seasonal filling in a short pastry case.
Bite-sized vegetable skewers: the simplest thing on the tray and the first to go.
Salads, kachumber and cold mezze
Three to five on a buffet. During Paryushan, leafy items come off the list — say so when you brief us and we build the salad round from pulses, sprouts and fruit instead.
Green salad / kachumber: cucumber, tomato and lemon, cut fresh on site.
Moong Sprout Salad: sprouted moong with lemon and coriander.
Three Beans Salad: mixed beans in a light dressing.
Rajma Salad: kidney beans, tomato, coriander.
Lentil Salad: cooked lentils, herbs, olive oil.
Quinoa Salad: quinoa with herbs and a lemon dressing.
Kale Salad with Walnuts, Mango & Strawberry: the one guests photograph.
Baby Spinach Salad with Pomegranate: sweet, sharp and quick to plate.
Indian Summer Salad: seasonal vegetables, chaat masala, lime.
Watermelon and Avocado Salad: for outdoor events in the heat.
Thai Spinach Nut Salad: peanut dressing, chilli, lime.
Greek Salad: cucumber, tomato, olives, feta.
Hommos: chickpea and tahina, made without garlic for a Jain menu.
Moutabal: smoked aubergine and tahina.
Muhammara: roasted pepper and walnut, sweet and smoky.
Tabbouleh: parsley-led, lemon-heavy, no onion.
Quinoa Tabbouleh: the gluten-conscious version of the same dish.
Soups
One soup on a buffet, two at a winter wedding.
Coriander Lemon: clear, sharp, the standard Indian-wedding opener.
Sweet Corn: thick and mild, the safe choice for a mixed table.
Cream of Tomato: finished with cream and basil.
Clear Vegetable: light broth with above-ground vegetables only.
Broccoli: blended, with a little cheese if you want it richer.
Paneer: one named line on every menu
Every Indian-vegetarian package carries paneer as its own line, and Jain hosts expect it. One on a buffet, two at a wedding.
Paneer Kadai: peppers, tomato and crushed spice, cooked dry in the kadai.
Paneer Butter Masala: the sweet tomato-cream gravy, built without onion.
Palak Paneer: spinach purée and paneer cubes.
Paneer Tikka Masala: grilled paneer folded back into a spiced tomato gravy.
Muttar Paneer: peas and paneer, the everyday version done properly.
Methi Malai Muttar: fenugreek, cream and peas — the mildest of the group.
Jain Tawa Paneer: griddled on the tawa, no onion, no ginger-garlic paste.
Baked Paneer: set under cheese and baked, popular at buffets.
Soya Chaap Makhani: soya chaap in a makhani gravy, for a heavier plate.
Dal
One named dal per menu. The tempering is where the Jain build shows: cumin and asafoetida, not a garlic tarka.
Jain Dal Makhani: slow-cooked black lentils, no onion or garlic in the base.
Dal Tadka: yellow lentils under a cumin and asafoetida tempering.
Dal Khichdi: dal and rice cooked together, soft and comforting.
Daal Palak: lentils with spinach, lighter than makhani.
Gujarati Daal: sweet-sour toor dal with jaggery and kokum.
Rasawala Moong: thin, soupy moong, eaten with rotla.
Paanch Kathol: five pulses cooked together, a Jain festival staple.
Kadhai Daal: cooked down with peppers and tomato.
Dal Baati Churma: the Rajasthani set piece — baked baati, dal and sweet churma.
Sabzi and seasonal vegetables
One or two vegetable lines per menu, chosen for what the market has that week, not fixed year-round.
Jain Mix Veg: above-ground vegetables only, in a light tomato gravy.
Gatte ki Sabji: Rajasthani besan dumplings in spiced yoghurt — the classic no-root main.
Jain Kofta Curry: koftas bound with banana and paneer instead of potato.
Ker Sangri: desert berry and bean, dried and revived — Rajasthani and naturally Jain.
Bharela Bhinda: okra stuffed with spiced besan.
Bhindi Masala: sliced okra cooked dry so it stays crisp.
Kaju Karela: bitter gourd with cashew, sweet against bitter.
Tindora Capsicum: ivy gourd and peppers, stir-fried.
Cauliflower & Nuts: florets with cashew and raisin.
Chole (Chana Masala): chickpeas in a dark, tamarind-edged gravy.
Jain Chole Bhature: with fried bhature, no onion in the chole.
Vegetable Manchurian: Indo-Chinese, built without onion or garlic.
Baby Corn Manchurian: crisper and milder than the mixed-vegetable version.
Sarson da Saag with Makke di Roti: mustard greens and corn bread, a winter menu only.
Continental and plant-based mains
Three or four of these turn a Jain buffet into something a mixed international guest list reads as a full menu, not a diet.
Baked Bell Pepper filled with Quinoa Stuffing: a plated vegan main that holds its shape.
Vegetable Ratatouille: courgette, aubergine and pepper, built without onion or garlic.
Italian Roasted Vegetables with Herbs: plain roasted, and the tray that empties first in summer.
Grilled Mixed Vegetables with Pesto Sauce: pesto made without garlic.
Cauliflower Provencal: roasted with tomato, olive and herbs.
Vegetable Szechuan: hot, dark and glossy.
Thai Coconut Chickpeas Curry: coconut milk, lime leaf, mild heat.
Thai Vegetable Curry: green or red, with jasmine rice alongside.
Spicy Tofu with Creamy Coconut Sauce: the protein line on a fully vegan menu.
Red Tofu Curry with Mushrooms: deeper and smokier than the green.
Mushroom Tofu Stroganoff: creamy, served over rice or pasta.
Risotto (Vegetable / Mushroom / Butternut): finished at a live station or plated.
Roasted Vegetable Couscous: a good room-temperature dish for outdoor events.
Stuffed Grape Leaves: rice, herbs and lemon, rolled by hand.
Pasta and noodles
One or two lines. Children's tables and international guests both look for this course first.
Spaghetti in Creamy Tomato Sauce with Pesto: vegan as written.
Creamy Pepper and Tomato Pasta: vegan, and the mildest of the group.
Creamy Butternut Squash Pasta with Pine Nuts: autumn and winter menus.
Vegetable Lasagna: layered and baked, cut at the buffet.
Penne Arrabiata with Parmesan Cheese: the sharp, hot option.
Penne Pomodoro: tomato and basil, nothing else needed.
Macaroni al Pesto: garlic-free pesto for a Jain brief.
Fusilli Pasta with Vegetables: seasonal, tossed light.
Fettuccine Alfredo: the richest thing on the pasta line.
Spinach Ravioli: filled pasta under a light tomato sauce.
Hakka Tofu Noodles: the Indo-Chinese noodle line, no onion.
Teriyaki Mushroom & Broccoli Noodles: sweet-savoury and quick to serve.
Vegetable Chow Mein: the counter favourite at a mixed buffet.
Triple Schezwan Rice: rice, noodles and sauce in one bowl.
Rice, biryani and khichdi
One rice line per menu, two at a wedding. The regional name matters — a Handi Hyderabadi and a plain vegetable biryani are not the same dish.
Handi Hyderabadi Biryani: sealed and dum-cooked, the wedding centrepiece.
Vegetable Biryani: lighter, layered with fried paneer and cashew.
Jain Pulao: no onion, no root, whole spice carrying the aroma.
Green Peas Pulao: the everyday rice at a Gujarati table.
Peas Pilaf: buttery, mild, good under a heavy gravy.
Jeera Rice: cumin, ghee, basmati.
Lemon Rice: south Indian, sharp, good cold as well as hot.
Steamed Basmati Rice: plain, and worth a place on every menu.
Jain Khichdi: moong and rice, the dish most Jain families ask for by name.
Moong Daal Khichdi: soft, mild, served with kadhi.
Vagharela Khichdi: tempered and spiced, a meal on its own.
Fada Khichdi: cracked wheat instead of rice.
Breads
Two breads on a standard menu, three at the top of the range, cooked through service, not stacked in advance.
Naan (Plain, Butter, Masala): off the tandoor, brushed as it comes.
Lachha Paratha: layered and flaky.
Jain Stuffed Paratha: filled without potato — paneer, peas or methi instead.
Missi Roti: gram flour and wheat, spiced into the dough.
Kulcha: soft, leavened, good with chole.
Chapati / Rotli: thin, made to order at the tawa counter.
Whole Wheat Poori: puffed and fried, for a festival menu.
Bhakri: thick, rustic, Kathiawadi.
Bajari Rotla: pearl-millet flatbread, eaten with ghee and jaggery.
Methi Thepla: fenugreek-laced, the travel bread every Gujarati family knows.
Pooran Poli: sweet lentil-filled bread, festival food.
Makke di Roti: corn bread, served with sarson da saag.
Raita, chutneys and accompaniments
Raita is a named line, not a garnish. Three or four accompaniments finish the table.
Boondi Raita: the default, and the one most guests reach for.
Cucumber Raita: cooling, cumin-seasoned.
Mixed Vegetable Raita: built from above-ground vegetables only.
Papad: roasted or fried, plated at the last moment.
Mint chutney: fresh, made without garlic.
Spicy green chutney: chilli-forward, for the chaat counter.
Sweet tamarind chutney: the sweet half of every chaat.
Mixed pickle: sharp, oily, in small bowls down the table.
Live stations
One or two stations for an intimate event; three to five build a wedding. Each needs power, a working surface and a chef standing at it, so tell us the venue's limits early.

Two of them are settled by the venue rather than the menu, and it is worth asking before the menu is signed. The live tandoor burns charcoal, so it stands outdoors on a villa plot — Dubai Municipality’s barbecue guidance is explicit that coal is never lit indoors or in an enclosed space — and on a beach it needs a permitted private event or the beach club’s own sign-off. For a rooftop or a desert camp, myCHEF confirms the position with the building management or the site operator before quoting. It does not travel to a yacht or an apartment: no additional gas or fuel cylinder may be brought aboard a boat (D-Marin Art. 53.1(a)), and Emaar’s vertical-community rules bar barbecues, grills or cooking equipment of any kind from balconies and terraces whatever the fuel. Where the tandoor cannot come, the naan, kulcha and paneer skewers are baked in the licensed partner kitchen and finished to order on an induction counter, so the breads still arrive hot and brushed in front of guests. The saj is the easier of the two to place: a gas saj follows the same cylinder rules, but an electric domed saj carries no flame and runs indoors, on a terrace or in an apartment off a single dedicated socket, which is how the zaatar and cheese breads keep their live counter in a tower. On a yacht both stay ashore, and the breads are baked in the licensed kitchen, warmed in the galley and served with the rest of the menu.
Live Pani Puri / Sev Puri Station: assembled in front of the guest, Jain fillings only.
Dosa Counter: batter poured to order, with sambar and chutneys.
Tawa Counter: rotis and parathas cooked through service.
Live Tandoor for Starters: paneer and vegetable skewers off the coals.
Live Indian BBQ Station — Paneer Tikka Skewers: grilled and served straight to the plate.
Indo-Chinese Counter: Manchurian and noodles tossed in the wok.
Kathi Roll / Bread & Rolls Station: filled and rolled to order.
Live Pasta Station: tagliatelle, farfalle or penne finished with pesto, tomato or cream.
Live Asian Station: vegetable tempura and spring rolls fried on the spot.
Live Saj Station: zaatar, labneh and cheese on the domed saj.
Live Sweet Crepe Station: chocolate, strawberry, banana, pineapple, nuts.
Live Savory Crepe Station: olives, grilled vegetables, mushroom.
Live Pancake Station: for a brunch or a children's table.
Gola Station: shaved ice and syrups, the outdoor-event favourite.
Kulfi Falooda Counter: assembled in the glass in front of the guest.
Live Luqaimat & Regag Station: fried to order, finished with date syrup.
Mithai
One sweet on a short menu, two or three at a festival. All eggless, and made without honey.
Gulab Jamun: warm, in syrup, the one nobody skips.
Ras Mallai: chenna discs in cardamom milk.
Rasgulla: light, spongy, served chilled.
Jalebi: fried to order and eaten hot.
Jalebi with Rabri: the richer pairing, for a wedding.
Suji Halwa: semolina and ghee, the temple-prasad sweet.
Rice Kheer: slow-cooked with cardamom and nuts.
Vermicelli Kheer: quicker, lighter, served warm or cold.
Ada Payasam: Kerala-style, with jaggery.
Paal Payasam: milk and rice, reduced slowly.
Firni: set in clay bowls, chilled.
Gujiya: filled pastry crescents, festival food.
Kulfi / Falooda: dense frozen milk, cut and served with vermicelli.
Desserts: Arabic, international and eggless
Eggless is stated separately from vegan here, because a Jain host and a vegan guest are asking two different questions.
Luqaimat: crisp dumplings, finished with date syrup, no honey.
Awamat with Date Syrup: the Levantine version of the same idea.
Baklava: layered phyllo, pistachio or walnut.
Basboussa: semolina cake, soaked and cut into diamonds.
Mouhalabieh with Orange: milk pudding, light after a heavy menu.
Umm Ali: warm bread pudding with nuts and cream.
Apple Crumble: baked in trays, served with cream.
Chocolate Brownies with Nuts: cut small for a dessert table.
Assorted Mini Pastries: the low-effort, high-coverage sweet round.
Fresh fruit platter and fruit canapés: seasonal, cut on site.
Eggless cakes and desserts: the whole dessert range built without egg.
Dairy-free chocolate mousse: for vegan guests at the same table.
Raw and plant-based desserts: dates, nuts and cacao, nothing baked.
Thalis, meal boxes and set formats
Where a buffet is the wrong shape — a working lunch, a temple gathering, a family sitting down together — a composed plate does the job better.
Ultimate Jain Thali: mixed dal, a paneer curry, two seasonal vegetable curries, flavoured or plain rice, fresh rotis or parathas.
Rajasthani Thali: dal baati churma, gatte ki sabji and ker sangri on one plate.
Jain Royal Meal Box: the full composed box, sweet included.
Jain Executive Meal Box: the office-lunch format, packed to travel.
Jain Express Delight Box: the lighter, quicker box for a short break.

add_block.new_heading: How do you keep the food strictly Jain on the day?
new_paragraphs: We keep it strict with a written brief, a dedicated prep setup and a confirmation with your family before service. Jain preparation rules and separation are agreed with the household in advance — which items are excluded, whether after-sunset cooking is a concern, and how strict the interpretation runs. The chef then works from separate utensils, fresh oil and clean surfaces so nothing crosses over from non-Jain ingredients. We are honest about what this means: a shared venue kitchen carries more risk than a controlled setup, so we plan the format around keeping the Jain food genuinely uncontaminated.
